npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"npm publish"* OR *"npm login"* OR *"npm adduser"* OR *"npm token create"* OR *"npm token revoke"*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.NPMRC))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(npm\\s+(publish|login|adduser|whoami)|npm\\s+token\\s+(create|revoke))", field=CommandLine)) OR (#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\.npmrc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as instructed by the GitHub blog during upgrade prep
  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Baileys messages.upsert with requestId field — exploitation marker (CVE-2026-48063) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-48063 in Baileys (WhatsApp Web library) by hunting for the application-log signature documented in the advisory's workaround section: a messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field. The advisory tells defenders to drop exactly these events as the only practical mitigation, so their presence on a vulnerable build is a direct exploitation marker. Rationale: Advisory 'Workarounds' section explicitly names dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field as the only real workaround — making that exact field combination the highest-fidelity exploitation signature the article gives us. Cross-referenced patch commit 3beb08ee and the GHSA advisory page. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1566.003 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched Baileys (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) still emitting a benign requestId on legitimate placeholderResendMessage flows during normal history recovery
  • Custom Baileys forks that legitimately use requestId for in-house tracing/observability tagging
  • QA / staging debug logs where placeholderResendMessage is intentionally fuzzed to test resilience
  • Alternative WA libraries (whatsapp-web.js, venom-bot) emitting the substring 'messages.upsert' in their own log shape without the Baileys vuln
Suppression filter
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("version=7.0.0-rc12", "version=7.0.0-rc13", "version=6.7.22", "version=6.7.23"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the Baileys version on the alerting host (npm ls baileys / cat node_modules/baileys/package.json). If <7.0.0-rc12 or <6.7.22, treat the requestId-bearing upsert as an exploitation attempt; capture the SyslogMessage and the offending requestId for IR. Step 2 — Contain: terminate the Node.js process owning the WA socket and revoke the linked-device session inside the WhatsApp mobile app — this invalidates the attacker's spoofing channel and forces re-pair. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every host running the vulnerable npm package; pivot on the requestId pattern across 30 days of forwarded app logs to find earlier silent spoofing that the upsert handler accepted.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("node", "nodejs", "pm2") or SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert" and SyslogMessage has "requestId"

Baileys app state sync corruption — repeated reconciliation failures from a single peer AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the second documented impact of CVE-2026-48063: 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares'. Hunts for clusters of app-state-sync validation errors, key-share rejections, or sync rollbacks emitted by Baileys-based Node.js services within a short window — the cascading-correction pattern the advisory describes. Rationale: Advisory Impact paragraph explicitly cites 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares' and 'no workarounds for the app state sync jamming' — making clusters of app-state-sync failures the natural detectable signature of the second exploit path. Anchor strings (appStateSync, AppStateSyncKey, fetchAppStateSyncKey) come from the public Baileys source tree referenced by patch commit 3beb08ee. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network instability causing transient WA socket disconnects and benign appStateSync retries
  • Legitimate bulk-message flows that trigger normal sync reconciliation
  • Account using multiple linked devices simultaneously, producing concurrent appStateSync deltas
  • Baileys upgrade in progress where a new key-share format temporarily mismatches cached state
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host runs a vulnerable Baileys version (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22). If yes and >=3 appStateSync failures occurred in <10 min from the same session, treat as exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: stop the affected Node.js service, wipe the local Baileys auth/keys directory, and re-pair via QR / 8-digit code from the mobile device. Do NOT restore from snapshot — local state may already be corrupted. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the WA session ID / Baileys auth folder across all other hosts using shared credentials; check for messages.upsert + requestId hits (UC1) on the same time window.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| summarize ProcessStarts = count(), FirstStart = min(Timestamp), LastStart = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ProcessStarts >= 3
| order by LastStart desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("appStateSync", "AppStateSyncKey", "app-state-sync", "syncAppState", "fetchAppStateSyncKey")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("fail", "error", "invalid", "rollback", "reject", "mismatch", "timeout")
| summarize FailCount = count(), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount >= 3
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND (appStateSync OR AppStateSyncKey OR fetchAppStateSyncKey OR syncAppState) AND (fail OR error OR invalid OR rollback OR reject OR mismatch)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")

| where fail_count >= 3

Vulnerable Baileys npm package presence (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22) — fleet inventory hunt AIWeaponization High
Identifies hosts with a vulnerable Baileys install on disk so the SOC can drive patch adoption for CVE-2026-48063. Pivots on node_modules/baileys and node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys package.json writes captured by EDR file telemetry. Escalates internet-facing services that remain unpatched >7 days post-advisory. Rationale: Article specifies the exact vulnerable npm package names (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) and the version cut-offs (<7.0.0-rc12, <6.7.22). The file-event signature on node_modules/<pkg>/package.json is the most reliable cross-EDR fingerprint of installation regardless of host OS. Cross-checked the GHSA advisory and the npm registry pages. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://www.npmjs.com/package/baileys • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@whiskeysockets/baileys
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched installs (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) — file presence alone doesn't reveal version; analyst must read package.json contents
  • Developer workstations with the package installed for local testing (lower severity than production hosts)
  • Containers built FROM a vulnerable layer but never run in production
  • Old node_modules trees inside a backup snapshot mounted on a sandbox host
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for every alerting host, read node_modules/baileys/package.json (or @whiskeysockets variant) and extract the version field. Hosts on >=7.0.0-rc12 or >=6.7.22 are patched — close. Otherwise continue. Step 2 — Contain: prioritise internet-facing or production WA-bot services; schedule package upgrade via npm install baileys@^7.0.0-rc12 (or 6.7.22 for the v6 line) and redeploy. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference against UC1 (messages.upsert + requestId) and UC2 (appStateSync failures) on the same hosts to confirm whether exploitation already occurred before the patch lands.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "baileys"
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Writers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5) by DeviceName, FolderPath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "baileys"
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc

Baileys Node.js exceptions during protocolMessage parsing — exploit-path indicator AIExploitation Medium
Detects malformed protocolMessage parsing failures inside Baileys-based services: TypeErrors, RangeErrors, buffer overruns, or unhandled promise rejections referencing protocolMessage or its decoder paths. The advisory pins the root cause to maliciously crafted protocolMessage payloads, so deserialisation exceptions on inbound payloads are an early-stage exploitation signal. Rationale: Article maps exploitation to a 'maliciously crafted protocolMessage payload' — clustered Node.js deserialisation exceptions referencing protocolMessage in Baileys-tagged log lines are the natural exploit-path telemetry. Exception strings (TypeError / RangeError / UnhandledPromiseRejection / ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS) are V8-canonical and emitted by every Node.js runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Baileys upgrade in flight — old serialised state on disk + new code triggers parsing exceptions on first launch
  • Truly malformed inbound messages from buggy peer clients (not exploit) that still throw RangeError on the wire
  • Unrelated Node.js exceptions on the same process that mention 'TypeError' but aren't in the Baileys protocolMessage path
  • Local development environments with verbose debug logging producing benign caught-and-logged exceptions
Suppression filter
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("DeprecationWarning", "ExperimentalWarning", "npm WARN"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the stack trace from the offending SyslogMessage; confirm the failing frame is inside Baileys (node_modules/baileys/lib/Socket/messages-recv or similar). If yes, treat as exploitation attempt. Step 2 — Contain: stop the affected Node.js service to halt continued exploitation of the same payload pattern; capture the inbound raw message buffer if logged for IR sample. Step 3 — Hunt: correlate the exception timestamp with UC1 (messages.upsert + requestId) within 60s; sweep across all Baileys hosts for the same stack frame to find scaled exploitation attempts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| summarize ProcessStarts = count(), FirstStart = min(Timestamp), LastStart = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ProcessStarts >= 3
| order by LastStart desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys", "protocolMessage")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("TypeError", "RangeError", "SyntaxError", "UnhandledPromiseRejection", "Cannot read prop", "out of range", "ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS")
| summarize ExcCount = count(), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where ExcCount >= 2
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys" OR protocolMessage) AND (TypeError OR RangeError OR UnhandledPromiseRejection OR "Cannot read prop" OR "out of range")
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RawProcessId, CommandLine], function=count(as=launches))
| launches > 3
APPLICATION
index=app OR index=nodejs OR index=application (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys" OR "protocolMessage") ("TypeError" OR "RangeError" OR "SyntaxError" OR "UnhandledPromiseRejection" OR "Cannot read prop" OR "out of range" OR "ERR_BUFFER_OUT_OF_BOUNDS")
| bin _time span=5m as bucket

Fake messages.upsert from unknown peer JID — Baileys session-list anomaly AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the spoofed-message impact of CVE-2026-48063: messages.upsert events whose source peer JID isn't part of the established Baileys session peer list, or where decryption/MAC verification failed but the upsert still fired. These are the article's 'fake message key and payload' artefacts that the patch in commit 3beb08ee now rejects. Rationale: Advisory states the exploit lets an attacker 'trigger a fake messages.upsert event with a fake message key and payload' — the natural signature is upsert log lines accompanied by peer-list or cryptographic-verification failures emitted by Baileys (the patch in commit 3beb08ee adds exactly these rejection paths). Anchor strings (verifyMessage, decryption failed, MAC verification, remoteJid mismatch, unknown jid) come from Baileys' source tree and Signal-protocol-derived error vocabulary. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1566.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Group chat where a participant left and rejoined causing a transient JID-not-in-session warning
  • Mobile device re-pair while the Baileys session was active producing benign decryption-failed lines
  • Bot temporarily disconnected during sender-key rotation, replaying with stale state
  • Custom Baileys patches that intentionally log verifyMessage warnings without dropping the event
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: extract the offending JID from the SyslogMessage; check whether it appears anywhere else in the host's WA session history. If never seen, treat as spoof. Step 2 — Contain: terminate the Baileys Node.js process, revoke the linked-device in the WhatsApp mobile app, and wipe local auth/keys before re-pair. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the spoofed JID across all hosts using the same WA number; cross-reference against UC1 hits and UC4 exception bursts in the same time window — a clean triple-positive is a confirmed exploitation chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("web.whatsapp.com", "g.whatsapp.net", "mmg.whatsapp.net") or RemotePort in (443, 5222)
| summarize WaConnections = count(), Peers = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where WaConnections > 0
| order by bin_Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("unknown jid", "jid not in session", "unknown peer", "verifyMessage", "decryption failed", "MAC verification", "remoteJid mismatch", "unrecognised participant")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND "messages.upsert" AND ("unknown jid" OR "jid not in session" OR "unknown peer" OR verifyMessage OR "decryption failed" OR "MAC verification" OR "remoteJid mismatch")
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=5222) ContextImageFileName="*node*"
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(as=connections))
APPLICATION
index=app OR index=nodejs OR index=application (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") "messages.upsert" ("unknown jid" OR "jid not in session" OR "unknown peer" OR "verifyMessage" OR "decryption failed" OR "MAC verification" OR "remoteJid mismatch" OR "unrecognised participant")
| stats count as anomalies values(source) as sources first(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen by host process
| where anomalies >= 1

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    product: windows
detection:

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JDY botnet C2 check-in URI paths (/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status, /data/v2/pscan) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound HTTPS POSTs containing JDY's two hard-coded C2 URI paths used by the scanning malware to register a bot and submit port-scan results. These paths are unique to the JDY dispatcher / pscan endpoints documented by Black Lotus Labs. Rationale: Both URI paths are JDY-unique strings (per Lumen Black Lotus Labs IOC bundle): one is the bot's dispatcher check-in, the other submits scan results. They are not generic API paths and have no known benign use, so any single match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against Lumen's blog and BleepingComputer's coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193490/malware/jdy-botnet-evolves-after-kv-takedown-targets-military-networks.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA traffic replaying captured malware samples in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel researcher box doing controlled detonation against JDY infrastructure
  • Honeypot/decoy router emulating compromised devices for research
  • Penetration test using public JDY-emulation harness
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceHostName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","honeypot","researcher"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Validate the source device — if it's a SOHO router, Hikvision/Draytek/Ubiquiti device, or branch firewall, treat as confirmed JDY infection. Pivot on src IP to find all destinations contacted. Step 2 (contain): Block 149.248.3.38 and the resolved C2 host at egress firewall; isolate the device from production VLANs; pull a memory image if the device permits. Step 3 (hunt): Search 30 days back across CommonSecurityLog for any device that POSTed to these URIs; correlate with DNS queries to Tor exit relays; review inbound scanning patterns from your perimeter logs that match JDY's TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP probing fingerprint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","HttpConnectionInspected")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status", "/data/v2/pscan")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let JdyPaths = dynamic(["/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status","/data/v2/pscan"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any (JdyPaths)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet C2 Check-in URI Paths
id: 6f3b1d2a-9c44-4b78-9e0f-2a14d0c8b7e1
description: Detects outbound HTTP requests carrying JDY botnet's hardcoded C2 URIs /dispatch_service/v2/probe_status (bot check-in) and /data/v2/pscan (scan result submission).
references:
  - https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    cs-method: POST
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status'
      - '/data/v2/pscan'
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:cloudtrail OR source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.defender) (@http.url:(*\/dispatch_service\/v2\/probe_status* OR *\/data\/v2\/pscan*) OR @url.path:(*\/dispatch_service\/v2\/probe_status* OR *\/data\/v2\/pscan*) OR @RequestURL:(*\/dispatch_service\/v2\/probe_status* OR *\/data\/v2\/pscan*))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/.*/i
| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443}, field=aid, key=aid)
| regex("(/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status|/data/v2/pscan)", field=HttpHost)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, HttpHost], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status*" OR Web.url="*/data/v2/pscan*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where http_method="POST" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/dispatch_service/v2/probe_status*" OR Web.url="*/data/v2/pscan*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where http_method="POST" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Outbound connection to JDY Platypus payload server 149.248.3.38:13339 AIInstallation Medium
Detects any connection from an enterprise asset to JDY's hard-coded Platypus reverse-shell payload server at 149.248.3.38 on TCP/13339. Platypus is the open-source host-management tool the JDY operators use to manage compromised SOHO/IoT bots. Rationale: Lumen identifies 149.248.3.38:13339 as the Platypus host-management endpoint for JDY-compromised devices. Port 13339 alone is unusual enough that combining IP OR port gives both precision (exact IP) and a degraded-but-useful catch (port rotation). No legitimate business workflow connects enterprise endpoints to this address. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://securityaffairs.com/193490/malware/jdy-botnet-evolves-after-kv-takedown-targets-military-networks.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/china-linked-jdy-botnet-uses-1500-soho-and-iot-devices/
ATT&CKT1105 T1571 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher manually inspecting the JDY IP from a sanctioned analyst workstation
  • Threat-intel platform automated IOC fetch hitting the IP for enrichment
  • Internal scanner (Nessus/Qualys) configured to probe the IP as part of an IOC validation sweep
  • Sandbox detonation traffic from a controlled environment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","researcher","siem-enrich"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source device class — non-Windows IoT/SOHO devices (Hikvision NVR, Draytek, Ubiquiti, Linksys) are presumed compromised. Check connection duration, byte counts, and whether traffic is bi-directional (Platypus reverse-shell shape). Step 2 (contain): Block 149.248.3.38 globally at egress; null-route port 13339 to public destinations; physically segment any SOHO/IoT device that initiated the connection. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 90-day flow logs for the same src IP contacting any Tor entry guard or directory authority; check for inbound CVE-2026-35616 scan attempts originating from JDY infrastructure; enumerate other compromised devices on the same subnet using JDY's `auditdy` process name (see related UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIP == "149.248.3.38" or (RemotePort == 13339 and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP == "149.248.3.38" or (DestinationPort == 13339 and DeviceAction in~ ("allow","accept","permit"))
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestURL),
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr == "149.248.3.38" or DstPortNumber == 13339
        | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct)
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet Platypus C2 Payload Server Connection
id: 4d2a8e6c-3f8b-4a91-bbd9-87c63a40e6f2
description: Detects outbound network connections to JDY botnet's hardcoded Platypus payload/management server 149.248.3.38 on TCP port 13339.
references:

(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:cloudtrail OR source:windows.defender) (@DestinationIp:149.248.3.38 OR @network.destination.ip:149.248.3.38 OR @destination.ip:149.248.3.38 OR (@DestinationPort:13339 AND @network.destination.ip:*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| RemoteAddressIP4="149.248.3.38" OR RemotePort=13339
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count(), limit=max)

# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, protocol, action, bytes

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="149.248.3.38" OR (All_Traffic.dest_port=13339 AND All_Traffic.action="allowed") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.transport All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

JDY Linux/MIPS malware process name 'auditdy' (auditd masquerade) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of a process named 'auditdy' on Linux systems. JDY's MIPS/MIPSEL implant masquerades as the legitimate Linux auditd daemon by using the slightly-misspelled name 'auditdy', which it uses both as its own process name and as a self-check string to avoid double-infection. Rationale: Per Lumen's IOC bundle, JDY uses 'auditdy' as its in-memory process name (typo of legitimate Linux auditd) and reads /proc to detect prior infections by matching this string. Single-event match is high-fidelity because the legitimate daemon is auditd, not auditdy — any hit is either JDY or a typo'd custom script worth investigating. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.mallory.ai/malware/019eb25c-b652-76c7-ad7f-2418398d0a17
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.004 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom in-house monitoring script accidentally named 'auditdy' by a sysadmin
  • Bash test harness referencing 'auditdy' in a comment or variable name
  • Security tool red-team simulating JDY for tabletop exercises
  • Tab-completion typo in an interactive shell
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("redteam","pentest") and DvcHostname !has "lab"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm host is Linux (especially MIPS/MIPSEL — embedded edge gateway or IoT). Pull the binary if still on disk (JDY self-deletes after launch, so check /proc/<pid>/exe and /proc/<pid>/maps). Capture hash and compare with Lumen IOC GitHub. Step 2 (contain): Kill the process tree, quarantine the host, dump memory if forensically valuable. Block egress to 149.248.3.38 and known JDY C2 ranges. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all Linux fleet for any process referencing 'auditdy'; pivot on parent process to find the dropper shell script; search for shell-script downloads of mips/mips64/mipsel/mipsel64 ELF binaries in the last 30 days; correlate with CVE-2026-35616 exploitation attempts that may have delivered the implant.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "auditdy" or ProcessCommandLine has "auditdy"
| where FileName != "auditd"

title: JDY Botnet 'auditdy' Process Masquerading as auditd (Linux)
id: 9a7e1b4d-2c63-4d57-89af-bd1029ee4af5
description: Detects execution of a process named 'auditdy' on Linux systems. JDY's MIPS/MIPSEL bot uses this misspelled-auditd name as its own process and as a string check to avoid double infection.
references:

Inbound CVE-2026-35616 FortiClient EMS exploitation attempts (JDY scanning) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for inbound exploitation attempts against Fortinet FortiClient EMS API auth bypass (CVE-2026-35616) — the specific CVE the article cites JDY weaponising shortly after public disclosure. Targets unauthenticated POST requests to the EMS API surface from JDY-class SOHO source IPs. Rationale: Article + Lumen explicitly call out CVE-2026-35616 (Fortinet FortiClient EMS API auth bypass, CVSS 9.1) as the disclosed CVE JDY scanned for within hours of release. Cross-checked with NVD, watchTowr, NetSPI write-ups confirming the EMS API surface as the attack vector. Hunting tier because JDY source IPs change constantly (1,500+ SOHO devices in US/BR/EU/Asia), so we rely on FortiClient EMS access shape, not IP allowlists. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-35616 • https://watchtowr.com/resources/fortinet-forticlient-ems-zero-day-cve-2026-35616-active-exploitation-underway/ • https://www.netspi.com/blog/executive-blog/critical-vulnerability/cve-2026-35616-cve-2026-21643-fortinet-forticlientems-overview-takeaways/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus, Qualys, Tenable) exercising EMS API in scheduled scan
  • FortiClient agent fleet beaconing in to EMS at scale (legitimate POST traffic)
  • Red team / pen test contracted to probe EMS exposure
  • BishopFox CVE-2026-35616-check tool run by internal security team
  • Misconfigured legitimate integration retrying after a 401
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<your-scanner-CIDR>"])) and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Tenable","Burp","Nuclei")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm FortiClient EMS version — patched releases (above 7.4.6) are not vulnerable; if 7.4.5 or 7.4.6 unpatched, treat as exposed. Pull the offending POST bodies from FortiGate / WAF / IIS logs and look for evidence of EKZ infostealer drop or admin account creation. Step 2 (contain): Restrict EMS API to management VLAN only, force credential reset for any admin used during the window, isolate EMS host pending forensics, patch immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Search EMS logs for newly created admin accounts, exported endpoint deployment packages, or downloaded MSI payloads (EKZ disguises itself as a Fortinet patch); sweep endpoints managed by EMS for the same period for unexpected MSI installs from EMS-pushed packages.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ConnectionSuccess")
| where LocalPort in (443, 8013)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Vendor has_any ("Fortinet","fortinet") or DeviceName has "ems" or DeviceName has "forticlient"
    | distinct DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| summarize HitCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, LocalPort
| where HitCount > 3
| order by LastSeen desc
let SuspectUA = dynamic(["curl","python-requests","go-http-client","Mozilla/5.0 (compatible"]);
CommonSecurityLog

| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" or DestinationServiceName has_any ("forticlient","ems","FortiClient EMS")
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/","/EMS/","/_login","/fmcli")
| summarize HitCount = count(), DistinctURIs = dcount(RequestURL), AnyURIs = make_set(RequestURL, 25), AnyUA = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 10)
          by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| where HitCount > 5 or DistinctURIs > 3
| order by HitCount desc

Anomalous high-volume TCP/UDP/ICMP scanning from internal SOHO/IoT device AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts for the scanning fingerprint of a JDY-compromised internal device — a non-Windows host (security camera, branch router, NVR, IP phone) generating high-volume short-burst probes across many distinct destinations and ports, including ICMP-assisted UDP probing characteristic of JDY's scanning engine. Rationale: Article: JDY's scanner adapts to its privileges — SYN scanning via raw sockets when root, falling back to standard TCP/TLS connections and UDP/ICMP probing otherwise. This shape (one IoT/SOHO source sending >500 distinct dests and >20 distinct ports in a 5-min window) is the unique fingerprint of a scanning bot, not a phone/camera/router doing legitimate cloud check-ins. The IoT-vendor filter (Hikvision/Draytek/Ubiquiti/Linksys/Mimosa/Araknis/Cisco RV) maps directly to the device classes Lumen names as JDY victims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://gbhackers.com/china-linked-jdy-botnet/
ATT&CKT1046 T1095 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal scanner (Nessus, Qualys, Rumble/runZero) deployed on an IoT-class VLAN by accident
  • NMS / network monitoring tool (LibreNMS, PRTG) doing wide TCP health checks from a multi-homed appliance
  • Network printer firmware update broadcasting to discover update servers
  • Video surveillance system performing legitimate ONVIF discovery
  • Conferencing kit (Polycom, Cisco WebEx) probing STUN/TURN servers globally
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys","tenable","runzero","librenms","prtg","solarwinds")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the scanning source — confirm it is an IoT/SOHO-class device (not a sanctioned scanner). Pull a sample of destination IPs/ports and check whether the targeting pattern matches CVE-2026-35616 (port 443/8013) or other recently-disclosed edge CVEs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device from corporate VLANs immediately, snapshot/factory-reset if owned, replace if compromised firmware is suspected (JDY persists across reboots on many platforms). Block all egress from the IoT VLAN to public destinations except known-good services. Step 3 (hunt): Run the auditdy and 149.248.3.38:13339 detections against the same source IP; check perimeter inbound logs for the source IP being scanned BEFORE compromise (look for the original infection vector); enumerate all devices of the same vendor/firmware version for additional infections.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 — handleMessage RCE endpoint probe AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) endpoint `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` that watchTowr Labs disclosed as the entry path to the `handleExecute()` backend command processor. The patched build redirects unauthenticated callers to the login page, so any successful 2xx on this endpoint from an external source is high-fidelity. Rationale: watchTowr Labs explicitly named `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` as the vulnerable endpoint that reaches the `handleExecute()` backend. Patched builds redirect unauthenticated requests to login, so successful 2xx hits from external IPs are near-binary evidence of exploit attempts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) probing the endpoint post-patch verification
  • Penetration test engagement against Sentry assets
  • Ivanti support engineer reproducing customer issue via vendor remote session
  • Security researcher operating internal lab Sentry instance
  • Pre-prod Sentry replica receiving baseline functional tests
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-IPs>", "<pentest-IPs>") and RequestClientApplication !contains "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !contains "Qualys"
Response runbook
Triage: confirm the destination IP belongs to a Sentry/MobileIron Sentry appliance and check whether it is patched to R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1+. Pull full HTTP request body if logged — exploit payloads carry MICS configuration syntax. Contain: if response was 2xx and source is external, block source IP at perimeter, take an EDR/disk image of the Sentry host, and rotate any credentials/certificates it stored. Hunt: search same Sentry for child shells spawned by the Sentry Java process (Runtime.exec equivalents), new local accounts, cron entries, /tmp drops, and outbound connections to attacker infrastructure within ±2h of the probe. Correlate with CVE-2026-10523 admin-creation traffic in the same time window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage" or RemoteUrl has "mics-config/handleMessage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10523 — authentication bypass admin account creation AIInstallation High
Detects newly-created administrative accounts on Ivanti Sentry hosts shortly after unauthenticated traffic to MICS configuration endpoints. CVE-2026-10523 (CVSS 9.9) lets a remote unauthenticated attacker create arbitrary administrative accounts, so unsolicited admin-account creation on an unpatched Sentry is the post-exploit fingerprint. Rationale: Article ties CVE-2026-10523 to creating arbitrary administrative accounts via unauthenticated requests, naming the same MICS endpoint as the entry vector. Correlating Sentry admin-account creation events with prior unauthenticated `/mics/api/v2/sentry/` probes elevates the signal far above generic account-creation noise. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003 T1190
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Sentry administrator provisioning a new admin user through the MICS console
  • Automated configuration management adding service accounts during upgrade
  • Vendor support session creating a temporary diagnostic admin
  • DR failover test recreating admin accounts on standby Sentry
  • Identity provider sync adding new admin role mapping
Suppression filter
| where AttackerIP !in ("<approved-scanner-IPs>") and SyslogMessage !contains "automated_provisioning"
Response runbook
Triage: list all admin accounts created on the Sentry in the last 14 days and validate each against ITSM change records or HR provisioning tickets. Pull the corresponding `/mics/` HTTP request bursts immediately preceding each creation event. Contain: disable any unverified admin accounts, force password reset on the rest, rotate Sentry-stored API keys/certs, and isolate the appliance pending patch to R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1+. Hunt: search MDM-managed device events for the attacker pivoting through Sentry (config push, app install, MDM command issuance), and check whether SSO/IdP federation tied to Sentry was abused.
let SentryHosts = DeviceInfo

    | where DeviceName has_any ("sentry", "mobileiron")
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;

    | where RemoteUrl has "mics-config/handleMessage" or RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/"
    | project ProbeTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, AttackerIP = RemoteIP;
SentryHosts

| project DeviceId, DeviceName, ProbeTime, AttackerIP
| order by ProbeTime desc
let ProbeWindow = 2h;
let Probes = CommonSecurityLog

    | where RequestURL has "mics-config/handleMessage" or RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/"
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SentryHost = DestinationHostName, SrcIP = SourceIP;
Syslog

| where SyslogMessage has_any ("adduser", "useradd", "new admin user", "role=admin", "AdminCreated")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiSandbox CVE-2026-25089 — WEB UI OS command injection AIExploitation Medium
Hunts crafted HTTP requests to FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI that exploit CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS 9.1), an improper neutralization of special elements (CWE-78) allowing unauthenticated OS command execution. Looks for shell-metacharacters and OS-command primitives in request URIs or bodies targeting FortiSandbox management interfaces. Rationale: Fortinet's advisory names FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI as the vulnerable surface, with CWE-78 (OS command injection) as the bug class. Combining target-host context (fortisandbox/fsa hostname) with classic command-injection primitives produces a focused hunt that survives variation across versions 4.4.x and 5.0.x. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner payload probes against FortiSandbox WEB UI
  • Fortinet TAC remote troubleshooting using diagnostic URLs
  • Bug-bounty/pentest engagement against Fortinet appliances
  • Custom integration script with poorly-encoded parameters
  • Security researcher PoC validation in lab
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-IPs>", "<fortinet-tac-IPs>")
Response runbook
Triage: identify the FortiSandbox version on the targeted host and check it against Fortinet PSIRT — 5.0.0–5.0.5 / 4.4.0–4.4.8 are vulnerable. Pull the full request URI + body and the HTTP response status; 2xx with a non-empty body from an external IP is high-confidence compromise. Contain: block the source IP at perimeter, snapshot the FortiSandbox, and pull config diff for unauthorized changes. Hunt: search the FortiSandbox host for unexpected outbound TCP to attacker IPs, new SSH keys, /tmp drops, and process executions outside the FortiOS user space. Patch to 5.0.6 / 4.4.9.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("fortisandbox", "/fsa/", "/sandbox")
| where RemoteUrl has_any (";id", ";wget", ";curl", "|sh", "$(", "`id`", "%3B", "%7C", "/bin/bash", "nc -e")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (DestinationHostName has_any ("fortisandbox", "fsa") or DeviceProduct has "FortiSandbox")
| where RequestURL has_any (";id", ";wget", ";curl", "|sh", "$(", "%3B", "%7C", "/bin/bash", "nc -e", ";cat /etc", ";uname")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAP NetWeaver SAML XML signature wrapping (CVE-2026-44748) AIExploitation Medium
Detects SAML AuthN payloads to SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP / ABAP Platform whose XML signature scope wraps tampered identity assertions — the exact pattern Onapsis described for CVE-2026-44748. Hunt focuses on multiple `<Assertion>` or `<Subject>` elements, signed-info / signature-mismatched IDs, and SAP-target endpoints (`/sap/*`, `/saml2/`, `/its/`). Rationale: Onapsis described CVE-2026-44748 as XML signature verification accepting tampered identity inside otherwise-signed SAML — classic XML Signature Wrapping. SAP-bound POSTs containing SAMLResponse with multiple Assertion blocks (signature scope mismatch) are the on-wire fingerprint; pair with SAP audit log review of the target SAP user that suddenly received tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html • https://onapsis.com/
ATT&CKT1190 T1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SAML IdP that emits multiple assertion blocks (rare but exists)
  • SAML federation testing during IdP migration
  • Pen-test engagement against SAP SSO
  • Misconfigured custom SAML middleware adding wrapper elements
  • Vendor-supplied SAP SSO connector with non-standard XML schema
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-IdP-IPs>") and SourceUserName !contains "federation-test"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the SAMLResponse XML from the request body and inspect for multiple `<Assertion>` blocks, Reference URIs that don't match Assertion IDs, or signatures whose canonicalization scope excludes the Subject. Cross-check the resulting SAP user session in SM20/RSAU audit logs. Contain: invalidate the SAP session, rotate the IdP signing certificate if confirmed, and block the source IP. Hunt: pivot to the SAP user's subsequent ABAP transactions (RFC calls, table reads on sensitive tables like USR02, PA0008) and look for parallel exploit attempts against the same NetWeaver host. Patch per SAP Security Note.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/sap/", "/saml2/", "/its/")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("SAMLResponse", "SAMLRequest")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (DeviceVendor has "SAP" or DestinationHostName has "sap" or RequestURL has_any ("/sap/", "/saml2/"))
| where RequestURL has_any ("SAMLResponse", "SAMLRequest") or Message has "SAMLResponse"
| extend AssertionDup = countof(tostring(Message), "<saml:Assertion") > 1
| where AssertionDup or Message has "Reference URI"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, Message, SourceUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Ivanti / Fortinet / SAP software inventory (TVM) — pre-patch versions AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts running affected versions of FortiSandbox, Ivanti Sentry, and SAP NetWeaver / Commerce Cloud / Data Hub that are exposed to the seven CVEs in this advisory. Uses Vulnerabilities CIM data populated by vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7, Defender TVM export) to drive patch prioritization. Rationale: Article enumerates exact pre-patch version ranges (FortiSandbox 5.0.0–5.0.5 / 4.4.0–4.4.8; Ivanti Sentry < R10.5.2 / R10.6.2 / R10.7.1; SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP / ABAP Platform / Commerce Cloud / Data Hub). Mapping the seven CVEs against installed-software inventory is the cheapest way to scope blast-radius and drive emergency patch waves. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ivanti-fortinet-and-sap-release-patches.html
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanner reports stale data on already-patched hosts (rescan needed)
  • Lab/dev environment intentionally kept on vulnerable version for testing
  • Vendor-supported appliance where customer cannot patch independently
  • Inventory deduplication issues double-counting clustered SAP nodes
  • Decommissioned hosts still in scanner snapshot
Response runbook
Triage: prioritise internet-facing hosts (IsInternetFacing == true) and the two CVSS-10/9.9 Ivanti Sentry bugs first, then FortiSandbox 9.1, then SAP. Cross-reference each finding with CMDB owner. Contain: for any unpatchable internet-facing host, gate it behind WAF rules blocking the article-specific endpoints (`/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage`, FortiSandbox WEB UI, SAML POSTs to SAP). Hunt: for each vulnerable host, run the matching exploitation-attempt UC over the last 30 days to confirm whether pre-patch exploitation already occurred.

| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)

| order by conn_count desc
